nt: Here, **sons** may mean “descendants,” since it would be unusual for Bela to have two sons named Gera, one named here and the other in verse 5. The term “sons” may similarly mean “descendants” in other places in this chapter.

The phrase **and Abihud** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Some scholars have suggested a slight change based on their belief that a consonant may understandably have been dropped in the process of copying from the text read aloud. This would yield the reading “even the father of Ehud.” This would make sense, since otherwise Ehud would be named in verse 6 without any prior introduction. It would also distinguish this **Gera** from the one in verse 5. Furthermore, according to [Judges 3:15](../jdg/03/15.md), the judge named Ehud was the son of a Benjaminite man named Gera. If there is a major Bible translation in your area and it follows this interpretation, you may wish to do the same in your translation. Alternate translation: [even the father of Ehud]
